summary: Defines the MIME objects used by the Common Indexing Protocol, and the methods and requirements for defining a new index type.

plainLanguage.summary: The exact shape of the boxes that index information travels in, plus rules for inventing new kinds of boxes.

what is the cip poll command
subtitle: The MIME message formats CIP servers use to poll, notify and exchange indexes, and the rules for new index types.

tldr.problem: Different kinds of indexes need different parameters, transports and referral rules, yet servers need one standard way to describe and exchange them.
tldr.mechanism: CIP wraps every request, response and index object in a MIME message under the application/index media type tree. It also lists what any new index type specification must address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the poll and datachanged commands, the response format, the index object type and the response codes that CIP version 3 servers use.

today: RFC 2652 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the MIME companion to the framework in RFC 2651.

sections.title: Introduction and Media Types
sections.content:
CIP passes indexes between servers that combine indexes or route queries. This document is read together with the framework in RFC 2651. Since there are many ways to index a database, there will be many index types with different transport needs, parameters and referral rules. Wrapping them all in MIME gives a standard way to state those differences. The document uses MUST and SHOULD as in RFC 2119.

CIP uses the application/index tree, split into four branches:

  • application/index.cmd.command for commands
  • application/index.response for responses
  • application/index.obj.type for index objects
  • application/index.vnd.xxx for vendor-specific uses

Commands, responses and types are 1 to 20 characters from letters, digits and the minus sign. They may be written case sensitively but must be compared case insensitively.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is put in a standard envelope, and the label on the envelope says whether it is a command, an answer, a list or something special from one company.

sections.title: DSI and Base-URI Syntax
sections.content:
A DSI is an identifier from the ISO/CCITT OID space. Real OIDs are unbounded, so CIP defines an ASCII form: integers separated by dots, with no leading zeros, and a total length that must not exceed 255 characters. An OID too long to fit cannot be used as a DSI. Implementations should treat the DSI as an opaque US-ASCII string, and two DSIs match when every number matches.

The base-URI parameter carries a list of URLs, as defined in RFC 1738, separated by whitespace (space, tab, carriage return or line feed).
sections.plainLanguage: A DSI is a collection's long ID number written with dots, like 1.3.5.7.9, and it has a length limit. The base-URI is a list of web-style addresses.

sections.title: Responses and Commands
sections.content:
Messages fall into requests, responses and results, all formatted as MIME. Every request must be followed by a response code unless no return path exists.

An application/index.response message has a required code parameter holding a 3-digit status. The first body line is a human comment that must not be depended on, and it is left empty if there is no comment. Later lines are reserved for each response to define.

Commands use application/index.cmd.command with optional type and dsi parameters. A command missing a parameter it needs gets code 502, and unrecognized extra parameters are silently ignored. The commands are:

  • noop has no parameters and is acknowledged with 200. It need not be signed.
  • poll needs type and dsi. A poller uses it to request an index object. The receiver answers 200 if it has nothing for that DSI or does not support that type, and 201 if output follows.
  • datachanged needs type and dsi. A pollee uses it to tell a poller that data changed. Its body is attribute and value pairs in RFC 822 style, defined by the index type. It is answered with 200 or 201 by the same rule as poll.

Other requests for mesh management and statistics are left as future work.
sections.plainLanguage: A poll says, "please send me your list." A datachanged says, "my list has changed." The answer is a short numbered reply, like 200 for "done" or 201 for "done, and more is coming."

sections.title: The Index Object Message
sections.content:
A server answers a poll with one or more index objects, always as a MIME multipart/mixed message. Each part is an application/index.obj.type object with two required parameters and no optional ones:

  • dsi, which globally and uniquely identifies the dataset the index came from
  • base-uri, one or more URIs that form the base of referrals made from the index

The type goes in the subtype name because different types may have different syntaxes. Body termination is set by the transfer protocol, and new protocols are encouraged to use SMTP-style termination.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for lists, the answer is one big envelope with a separate labeled envelope for each list. Each label names the collection and where to send people.

sections.title: Defining a New Index Type
sections.content:
Index objects are abstract, so each type needs its own specification. This RFC lists what that specification must cover. Registering a new type follows the MIME registration rules in RFC 2048.

  • Type-specific request bodies. The bodies of Poll and DataChanged must be fully specified.
  • Parameters. A new type name must be assigned whenever a change to the type's document is not completely backwards compatible. The spec should say how DSIs are generated and how the Base-URI applies to the index and changes during aggregation.
  • Aggregation. A type need not aggregate, but if not it must explain why and the effect on scalability. If it does, it must give the algorithm and its effect on mesh organization.
  • Referral generation. It must say how each access protocol makes a referral from the index. The example given is that RWhois and LDAP differ because LDAP uses a Distinguished Name.
  • Matching semantics. Authors must be clear about how a match is determined.
  • Security considerations must be included.

Authors may stay silent on how an index is derived from source data, because indexing methods can be proprietary. In a public mesh, though, every server should be able to parse the object, and aggregate it where needed.
sections.plainLanguage: If you invent a new kind of list, you must explain how to name it, how to merge it, how to point people to the right place and how to tell when a search matches.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Indexes can leak too much proprietary information unless carefully controlled, and the protocol needs external security services. Since CIP is MIME, MIME security solutions should be used wherever possible. CIP messages may be wrapped in a security multipart, and RFC 1847 security multiparts are recommended, with PGP/MIME (RFC 2016) as a practical choice.

A request without a valid signature is treated as anonymous. Security policy is otherwise implementation defined, though operations that could permanently harm a server's state should require a signed message from a trusted peer or administrator, and implementations should offer auditing. Answering anonymous poll requests is described as useful, since it encourages index builders to poll a server. A request rejected for authentication reasons gets a 530-series code.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can be signed like a letter with a seal. Servers can ignore unsealed letters that ask for anything risky, but may answer harmless questions from strangers.

sections.title: Response Codes
sections.content:
Appendix B lists the response codes for CIP version 3 servers. Implementors must use these exact codes, and undefined codes are treated as fatal protocol errors. For an unforeseen situation, adapt an existing code with a useful alternative comment rather than inventing a new one. The meaning of the digits follows RFC 821, Appendix E.

Appendix A holds the media type registration templates sent to the IANA for the index, command, response, object and vendor trees.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply numbers are a fixed menu. If something odd happens, pick the closest number and add a note instead of making up a new one.

items.label: Closing
items.desc: Connection closing in response to a close; transaction done.

items.label: Processed
items.desc: MIME request processed; expect no output.

items.label: Processed, output follows
items.desc: MIME request processed; read a response.

items.label: Try later
items.desc: Temporarily unable to process the request; retry later.

items.label: Unknown command
items.desc: Unknown or missing request in application/index.cmd.

items.label: Missing attributes
items.desc: Request is missing required CIP attributes.

items.label: Aborting
items.desc: Aborting connection for some unexpected reason.
